The first describes how things end up; the second helps you separate what happened (the action) from how everything is now (the state). You are joined by Lucía, a student from Medellín who arrives in Salamanca to do a master’s degree and settles into a residence inside a 17th-century building.
a2nq28: “Estar” + participle: the state an action leaves
1orm6jd: When someone does something, it leaves a result: limpiaron el baño → el baño está limpio; abrieron la ventana → la ventana está abierta. With “estar” + participle you describe that result, not the action. The participle works like an adjective and agrees with what it describes: “la puerta está cerrada”, “los cajones están cerrados”, “las luces están apagadas”.
1xx1heb: For a past state, use “estaba”: “Cuando llegué, la calefacción estaba encendida”. Remember the most frequent irregular participles: abierto, roto, hecho, escrito, puesto, vuelto, muerto, dicho, cubierto. With “limpiar”, “llenar”, “vaciar” and “secar” the adjective is preferred: “está limpio”, “está lleno”, “está vacío”, “está seco”.
gbhtjf: Ask yourself: am I talking about what someone did or about how the thing is now? If it’s how it is, “estar” + agreeing participle.
121g6x5: The participle agrees in gender and number with “las ventanas”.
vkpo1b: Haber, estar + gerund, quedar, tener and llevar
1wo6wcv: Don’t mix up three things. “He pintado la puerta” tells the action and the participle doesn’t change; “la puerta está pintada” describes the state and agrees; “estoy pintando la puerta” talks about the action in progress. With “quedar” or “quedarse” + participle you talk about the final state, often unexpected: “La persiana se quedó atascada”, “La reunión queda aplazada”.
1st4cy6: For progress so far, use “tener” + participle, which agrees with the object (“Tengo las maletas deshechas, pero no los libros”), and “llevar” + amount + participle (“Llevo tres cajas ordenadas”).

j0hcn5: “Ser” + participle: the action, with a date or an agent
bt9uw6: In news, history texts and official signs you’ll see “ser” + participle. It doesn’t describe a state but an action that happened, almost always with a date or with “por” + whoever did it: “El colegio fue fundado en 1611 por los jesuitas”, “La biblioteca fue inaugurada ayer por la alcaldesa”. The participle agrees here too: “Las obras fueron terminadas en marzo”.
41c12w: In conversation it is much more common to say the same in the active or with “se”: “Los jesuitas fundaron el colegio en 1611”, “El colegio se fundó en 1611”. At this stage what matters is that you understand “ser” + participle when you read or hear it, and that you can rephrase it.

1jfzyao: The participle in -ado: careful and relaxed forms
10xaxyo: In spontaneous speech in much of Spain, the “d” between vowels in the “-ado” participle weakens a lot or disappears: “estoy cansado” sounds almost like “estoy cansao”, “he terminado” sounds like “he terminao”. It’s normal in a conversation among friends, but in a formal situation or when reading aloud the soft “d” is pronounced.
wy1jqs: In “-ido” the “d” is kept more (“comido”, “salido”), and in feminine participles (“cansada”, “terminada”) it hardly ever disappears. When you speak, pronounce a soft “d”, with the tongue between the teeth and without closing completely: that way you sound natural in any register.
1kv77um: Always write “-ado”, even if you hear “-ao”: “cansado”, “terminado”. The forms “cansao” or “terminao” only appear in texts that imitate speech.
vbahnl: Four participles in “-ado”: don’t cut them short.

1r08zja: Lucía’s residence tells the history of the building on its website for new residents.
agij5c: The building where you live was built between 1611 and 1630 with Villamayor stone, the same golden stone as the cathedral. It was founded by a canon of the city as a college for students without means, who lived here for free in exchange for helping in the church next door. For two centuries the college was full of young people from all over Castile.
66rrc4: In the 19th century the building’s life changed completely. It was turned first into barracks and then into a grain store. By the mid-20th century it was already almost empty, and in 1978 it was closed because of the danger of collapse. It stood abandoned for almost forty years: the cloister roof had caved in, the windows were bricked up and the façade was covered in ivy.
73ys9o: In 2017 the City Council and the University signed an agreement, and the building was restored by a team of local architects. The work was finished in the summer of 2020, and the residence was opened in September, with the first forty students.
17gr3ps: Today the cloister is restored and open to residents, the rooms are equipped with heating and wifi, and the library is housed in the old chapel. Only the north wing is still closed: it is reserved for a future museum. If you look closely at the entrance, you’ll see that the canon’s coat of arms is still carved above the door.
